full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 a(n)=2n+\left\lfloor n\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac n4\right\rfloor
 \qquad(n\ge 1).
\]
We disprove the proposed recurrence by evaluating it at \(n=140\). At this index the conjecture asserts
\[
 a(161)=a(157)+a(144)-a(140).
\]
We will compute all four terms exactly.

Put
\[
 \alpha=\sqrt{\frac54}.
\]
Since \(5/4>0\), we have \(\alpha>0\) and \(\alpha^2=5/4\). Thus all the quantities below are nonnegative, and their order can be determined by comparing their squares.

First consider \(140\alpha\). Its square is
\[
 (140\alpha)^2=140^2\frac54=19600\cdot\frac54=24500.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
 156^2=24336<24500<24649=157^2.
\]
Because \(156\), \(140\alpha\), and \(157\) are nonnegative, it follows that
\[
 156<140\alpha<157.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \left\lfloor140\alpha\right\rfloor=156.
\]

For \(144\alpha\), we have
\[
 (144\alpha)^2=144^2\frac54=20736\cdot\frac54=25920.
\]
The adjacent integer squares satisfy
\[
 160^2=25600<25920<25921=161^2.
\]
Hence
\[
 160<144\alpha<161,
\]
and therefore
\[
 \left\lfloor144\alpha\right\rfloor=160.
\]

For \(157\alpha\), multiplying the relevant square comparisons by \(4\) avoids fractions. We have
\[
 4(157\alpha)^2=4\cdot157^2\frac54=5\cdot157^2
 =5\cdot24649=123245.
\]
Meanwhile,
\[
 4\cdot175^2=4\cdot30625=122500
 <123245
 <123904=4\cdot30976=4\cdot176^2.
\]
It follows that
\[
 175^2<(157\alpha)^2<176^2.
\]
All quantities being nonnegative, this gives
\[
 175<157\alpha<176,
\]
so
\[
 \left\lfloor157\alpha\right\rfloor=175.
\]

Finally, for \(161\alpha\),
\[
 4(161\alpha)^2=5\cdot161^2
 =5\cdot25921=129605.
\]
The neighboring square bounds are
\[
 4\cdot180^2=4\cdot32400=129600
 <129605
 <131044=4\cdot32761=4\cdot181^2.
\]
Thus
\[
 180^2<(161\alpha)^2<181^2,
\]
whence
\[
 180<161\alpha<181

after taking nonnegative square roots. Therefore
\[
 \left\lfloor161\alpha\right\rfloor=180.
\]

The rational floor terms are immediate:
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{140}{4}\right\rfloor=35,
 \qquad
 \left\lfloor\frac{144}{4}\right\rfloor=36,
 \qquad
 \left\lfloor\frac{157}{4}\right\rfloor=39,
 \qquad
 \left\lfloor\frac{161}{4}\right\rfloor=40.
\]
Indeed, the first two divisions are exact, while \(157=4\cdot39+1\) and \(161=4\cdot40+1\).

Substitution into the definition of the sequence now gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 a(140)&=2\cdot140+156+35=280+156+35=471,\\
 a(144)&=2\cdot144+160+36=288+160+36=484,\\
 a(157)&=2\cdot157+175+39=314+175+39=528,\\
 a(161)&=2\cdot161+180+40=322+180+40=542.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore the right-hand side of the proposed recurrence at \(n=140\) is
\[
 a(157)+a(144)-a(140)=528+484-471=1012-471=541,
\]
whereas its left-hand side is
\[
 a(161)=542.
\]
Thus
\[
 a(161)\ne a(157)+a(144)-a(140).
\]
Since \(140\ge1\), this is an admissible index in the universally quantified conjecture. Hence the assertion that
\[
 a(n+21)=a(n+17)+a(n+4)-a(n)
\]
holds for every \(n\ge1\) is false.
